title: GPU pool thrum — timeline & probing scratchpad
content:
Purpose:
This is a personal scratchpad to track the repeating low-amplitude instability we've been calling the 'thrum' in the eu-west dedicated GPU pool (gpu-dedicated-eu-west). Not a final report — a sequence log of probes, commands run, quick hypotheses, and short experiments. Use this to reproduce and hand off.

Summary of the observable symptom:
- Intermittent capacity chatter every ~60–120s: small-scale add/remove events (1-3 GPUs) that correlate with sudden drops in per-request throughput and long tail latencies.
- GPU pods report warmup spikes: initial token latency 80ms baseline -> occasional 1.5–2.0s spikes, then recovery in 10–30s.
- GPU utilization oscillates between ~5% and ~95% in short cycles for affected nodes (seen in prometheus node/gpu exporter).

Timeline (condensed):
2025-01-08 09:12 UTC — First customer report: batch infer job OOMing after 2m. Correlated with node churn.
2025-01-09 02:34 UTC — Observed automatic scale-down events in autoscaler logs with reason "low CPU" (curious, because our metric should be GPU util).
2025-01-11 18:07 UTC — Deployed additional logging and trace IDs for warmup path. Began collecting full kubelet logs.
2025-01-14 11:20 UTC — Ran controlled ramp test (see commands) and reproduced thrum under synthetic steady qps.
2025-01-15 14:45 UTC — Increased scale-up cooldown to 180s (experiment A). Reduced frequency but not eliminated.
2025-01-23 21:50 UTC — Rolled back cooldown tweak; tried jittering scale-signal (experiment B) — marginal improvement.
2025-02-03 07:10 UTC — Added prewarm KV-cache flag to new pool variant (experiment C). Warm spikes reduced for the variant, but still occasional thrum remains.

Commands / probes run (useful for repro):
- redwoodctl pool list --region eu-west
- redwoodctl pool inspect gpu-dedicated-eu-west --last-ops 200
- redwoodctl pool scale --pool gpu-dedicated-eu-west --target 8 --reason "probe-repro-20250114"
- kubectl get pods -n inference -l pool=gpu-dedicated-eu-west -o custom-columns=NAME:.metadata.name,STATUS:.status.phase,READY:.status.containerStatuses[*].ready,NODE:.spec.nodeName
- kubectl logs -n inference <pod> -c infer-runtime --since=15m | grep -E "warmup|kvcache|timing"
- ssh nodeX && journalctl -u kubelet -S "2025-01-14 11:00" | grep -E "evict|oom|attach|mount|throttle"
- prometheus queries used during tests:
  - avg_over_time(gpu_utilization_percent[2m])
  - increase(kube_pod_container_resource_requests{resource="nvidia.com/gpu"}[5m])

Representative log snippets (redacted):
- "2025-01-14T11:03:12Z WARN autoscaler: scale-down candidate: pool=gpu-dedicated-eu-west delta=-1 reason=low-cpu-metric"
- "2025-01-14T11:03:13Z ERROR scheduler: PodStartupFailure pod=inf-req-224 attach-volume: attach timed out"
- "infer-runtime warmup: kvcache-miss for prompt-prefix=~39ms; cold-init-add 132ms"
- "node-exporter: gpu0 util=7% -> 92% within 80s; process: runtime-worker pid=24833"

Hypotheses (ranked):
1) Metric mismatch: autoscaler using CPU-derived signal or aggregated metric that doesn't reflect GPU steady-state, causing undersized decisions for bursty workloads. Explains scale-downs labeled low-cpu.
2) False-negative readiness probes during cold-start (network hang to metadata or KMS) -> pods reported NotReady -> autoscaler/scheduler reacts -> small churn.
3) Shared node-level thrash (ephemeral storage pressure or blobstore attach contention) causing kubelet to evict or restart containers briefly -> transient loss of throughput.
4) Race between cache warmers and the request routing layer: when a freshly provisioned pod gets traffic before KV cache prime, latency spikes; the circuit triggers scale logic and we lose small capacity slices, amplifying the oscillation.
5) Orchestrator bug: scale-down policy does not respect recently added nodes (missing cooldown window) when combined with burst capacity.

Experiments and quick results:
- Experiment A: cooldown=180s on autoscaler (2025-01-15) -> event rate dropped ~30% but thrums persisted during sequence-length shifts.
- Experiment B: add 5–20s random jitter to scale decisions -> less synchronized removes but no elimination.
- Experiment C: create pool variant with --prewarm-kv=true and route 10% of traffic -> warm spikes reduced for canary; suggests cache warm path matters.
- Experiment D (failed): bumped min_ready_seconds in Deployment to 60s -> introduced higher tail latencies due to slower turnover; reverted.

Quick root-cause candidates to prioritize:
- Confirm which metric autoscaler is actually evaluating (CPU vs custom GPU util). If wrong metric, immediate fix.
- Trace Pod readiness transitions + attach/mount latencies to see if volume/mount timeouts correlate.
- Check cloud provider attach limits (Azure/GCP attachment throttling) around the timestamps.

Immediate mitigation actions tried and notes:
- Pin heavy steady customers to a dedicated-reserved pool for the weekend (manual routing). Reduced customer-visible errors.
- Temporarily disabled autoscaler burst mode (set max_burst=0) — decreased frequency but increased cost.
- Added a short prewarm step in inference gateway: hold first request for 150ms and route to warmed replica if present (cheap heuristic) — reduced 95th p99 for test canary.

Data to collect next (actionable):
- Full kubelet logs + attach logs for nodeX involved in a thrum window (collect 10 windows).
- Correlate prometheus series: node_disk_io_time, node_allocatable_ephemeral_storage, gpu_utilization, pod_ready_transitions (per-pod).
- Trace IDs for request paths that saw >1s warmup to see exactly which component stalled.

Next experiments to run (ordered):
1) Reproduce with synthetic steady qps that includes occasional long sequences (works already) and capture full traces.
2) Temporarily switch autoscaler to GPU-util-only policy for one test pool and observe change.
3) Increase scale-in stabilization window to 5m for one pool to see if chatter suppressed without affecting tail latencies.
4) Run node-level stress tests to provoke attach/mount contention (storage attach/release loop) and watch for kubelet eviction patterns.

Notes / observations (loose):
- The autoscaler logs that say "low-cpu" are suspicious; we should audit metric config.
- When thrum events happen, controllers.k8s.io events show short-lived "FailedScheduling: no nodes available" even though new nodes were being provisioned — might be labeling mismatch at node join.
- Some affected pods show repeated ImagePullBackOff around the same windows (coincidence?) — could be registry flakiness increasing startup time.

Hand-off checklist before we escalate to SRE dedicated debug run:
- Collect 10 thrum windows (timestamps) and attach GCP/Azure node lifecycle events.
- Confirm autoscaler metric configs and provide sample metrics used for decisions.
- Share this scratchpad + synthetic ramp script in the incident channel.

References / artifacts to include when sharing:
- repo: github.com/redwood-inference/inference-loadtests (ramp script: /scripts/gpu_thrum_ramp.sh)
- jira: INFRA-1427 (current ticket)

Endnotes:
This has the feel of a multi-factor small-signal oscillation (not a single catastrophic bug). The word 'thrum' helps me avoid conflating with big flaps — it's persistent, low amplitude, and amplifies under slight shifts in workload distribution. Use the experiments above as controlled knobs before doing large platform-wide changes.

-- Aisha
